title: Barings: The Bank That Died in a Weekend
note: Original dramatized dialogue. Dialogue is not a historical transcript; narration should be checked against primary records.

lines.speaker: director
lines.text: Tell me that number is wrong.

lines.speaker: analyst
lines.text: I checked it twice. It isn't.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: London. February nineteen ninety-five. A report lands on a director's desk at Barings, the bank that had financed empires and survived more than two centuries.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: For years, the young trader appeared to make money almost every day. London saw the profits. What it didn't see was the account where the losses went.

lines.speaker: analyst
lines.text: Account eight eight eight eight eight.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And that was the point. A hidden account. A trader who could place bets and help reconcile the books. And a dangerous illusion that the numbers always added up.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Then, in January nineteen ninety-five, an earthquake hit Kobe, Japan. Markets moved violently. Leeson's bets became more dangerous.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Every request for cash brought the bank closer to a question nobody wanted to ask. How much could one trader lose before the whole institution fell?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: By the end of February, Barings would collapse. The eventual loss was reported at roughly eight hundred and twenty-seven million pounds. But the truly shocking part wasn't the size of the loss. It was how long the system allowed it to remain hidden.
